text: CE-CERT data also do not constitute a robust sample, so the strength of their diversity will generate more robust results in the combined data section. Whereas FleetDNA distributions actually matched closely to CE-CERT for urban other roads in Figure 58, in Figure 65 we see a pattern typical of other source types with more hours driven in the morning and less in the evening for urban other roads on weekdays. On weekends, we see CE-CERT transit buses driving more in the morning and evening in a bimodal distribution that contrasts MOVES3 weekend defaults. Hour VMT fractions for CE-CERT transit buses Weekend data for other buses follow a similar temporal pattern to MOVES3 with more extreme lows and highs of the distribution, as seen in Figure 66. In common with other source types, on urban other roads on weekdays, CE-CERT drives more in the morning and less in the evening and does not display the two-peaked trend of MOVES3. Airport shuttles on urban freeways have a choppy distribution, spending more time in the mornings and evenings and less at midday compared to MOVES3. There are no other buses in FleetDNA, and thus this category will not be shown in the combined analysis. As there were only five buses in this data sample, we do not recommend making updates to MOVES3 based on these results. 85 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. Figure 66. Hour VMT fractions for CE-CERT other buses Figure 67–Figure 69 show the vocational VMT fractions by hour for CE-CERT. As in the FleetDNA vocational graphs (Figure 60 and Figure 61), each colored area for a vocation sums to one, which does not represent the weighting for the source type as a whole where a vocation containing fewer vehicles would have less input on the overall distribution. Again, if an individual vocation did not contain enough data in a given road-day type to be shown per the data density section, it is also excluded here; however, it would contribute in aggregate to the source type distribution. These charts are stacked area plots, so the area to analyze is the color visible. No distributions are hidden—i.e., they do not extend downward to the x-axis except for the lowest color, which we can see contact that axis. Figure 67 shows that line-haul and municipal trucks operate more in morning hours on weekday urban road driving, while food distribution trucks operate from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m. Interestingly, drayage appears rather evenly spread across all hours on weekdays, but seems to stop driving by 5 p.m. on weekends. Construction displays morning and afternoon peaking in distribution on weekday urban driving. Cement mixers tend to operate more in the afternoon on rural roads and in the morning on urban roads.
